title: Malik and Ahmad
hook: the Muwatta of Malik and the Musnad of Ahmad, early and vast
tomorrow: The four books of the Shia

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four Sunan, and your line: the six books. Can you still name all six on your fingers? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five, the end of the week.

Medina. A teacher sits in the city where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lived and was buried, with students gathered around him and a book he has written. Tradition says he kept working on it, revising and trimming, for a long time before he was satisfied. He called it al-Muwatta: the trodden path, the way made smooth by the people who walked it before. His name was Malik ibn Anas. Yesterday we stood in front of the six books. Today we step to the side of that shelf, to two collections that stand next to it and are counted among the early ones. Malik and Ahmad.
screen: `A TEACHER IN MEDINA.` → `THE TRODDEN PATH.` → `BESIDE THE SIX BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the Muwatta. It's arranged by topics of law, like the Sunan, but it holds more than the Prophet's words. Next to them, Malik records what Companions did, what the people of Medina practiced, and his own judgment on the question. For Malik, the way the city of the Prophet actually lived was itself a kind of witness. One short report from it is easy to carry: the Prophet said that he was sent to perfect good character. Second, a line of teachers. Tradition says al-Shafi'i studied the Muwatta with Malik, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal later studied with al-Shafi'i. Founders of schools of law, each one sitting in front of the one before. Third, the Musnad. Ahmad's book is vast, and it's built in a completely different way. Musnad means supported, propped up by a chain. Instead of chapters on prayer or trade, it's arranged by Companion: all the reports that came through one Companion, then all through the next. Want what Abu Bakr narrated? It's together. Want everything about prayer? You'll have to hunt through the whole book. Ahmad wasn't building a handbook. He was building an archive. Fourth, the people behind the books. Tradition remembers both men holding firm when rulers of their day pressed them to say or do what they believed was wrong, and both paid for it. A collection is never only paper. It's a life spent listening, and sometimes a life spent refusing.
screen: `THE MUWATTA: HADITH AND MEDINA'S PRACTICE.` · `MALIK, AL-SHAFI'I, AHMAD.` · `THE MUSNAD: ARRANGED BY COMPANION.` · `A LIFE SPENT LISTENING.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one hadith from the Muwatta. Settle, and breathe. Here it is again: the Prophet said he was sent to perfect good character. Say it slowly, in three pieces. Sent. To perfect. Good character. Notice what it doesn't say. Not sent to win arguments. Not sent to be admired. Character. Now look back over this week: the narrators' biographies, the scholars who traveled for one report, the fakes they exposed, the books they built. All that care, for lines like this one. Bring to mind one moment this week when your own character slipped, and one when it held. Just look at both, without a verdict. The bell holds the time.
Malik and Ahmad. The Muwatta, the trodden path of Medina, and the Musnad, the reports arranged by the Companion who told them. Today's word.

Your line: early collections. This week ran from the narrators to the books. Today, practice one piece of good character with the person who tests yours most. Tomorrow: the four books of the Shia. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Followers of the Maliki school study the Muwatta closely, and scholars across schools use Ahmad's Musnad as a large reference archive of reports arranged by Companion.

original.note: the trodden path: a way made smooth by those who walked it.

trapdoor: what you thought: two more names for the list of six.
what it means: two collections that stand beside the six books: Malik's Muwatta and Ahmad's Musnad.
what a scholar hears: the Muwatta weighs Medina's living practice alongside hadith; the Musnad files every report under the Companion who told it.

notes: Muwatta 47:8 ('I was sent to perfect good character'): confirm book and hadith numbering in the edition used; it is a balagh (Malik says it reached him).
'Muwatta' glossed as 'the trodden path, made smooth': confirm the gloss.
Tradition that Malik revised the Muwatta over a long period: framed as tradition; the commonly cited 'forty years' is left out under the claims rule.
Teacher line Malik → al-Shafi'i → Ahmad: framed as tradition; confirm.
'Both men holding firm when rulers pressed them, and both paid for it' alludes to Malik's flogging and Ahmad's ordeal in the mihna; kept general. Confirm.
'Counted among the early ones' follows the outline's 'early and vast'; no dates given. Confirm both are fairly called early relative to the six books.
